analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug list prices at the average price charged in six peer nations.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap drug list prices at average prices in six other developed countries was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has had no further action, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for drugmakers to charge a U.S. list price higher than the average list price for the same drug in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Drugmakers would have to report their prices in each country every year, and the government could fine them ten times the overcharge for every unit sold above the cap. Americans currently pay far more for the same drugs than people in these countries, so the cap would mainly lower prices for people who pay list price out of pocket.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay cash or list prices for prescription drugs, including uninsured people and those with high deductibles, because the cap would limit how high manufacturers set the starting price of a drug. In principle, lower list prices could also ripple into lower negotiated prices for everyone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients who pay cash for drugs

how_it_helps.text: Caps the U.S. retail list price of any covered drug or biological product at the average list price charged in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom.
Requires manufacturers to report list prices in the U.S. and each of the six reference countries annually, so the government can calculate and enforce the cap.
Imposes a civil monetary penalty on manufacturers of ten times the difference between the U.S. price and the six-country average, charged for each unit sold above the cap.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. list prices would be forced down to a foreign average, reducing what they can charge. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that rely on rebate formulas tied to high list prices could also see that income stream squeezed.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps list prices, but many insured Americans pay negotiated prices shaped by rebates rather than list prices, so the cap's benefit to people with good insurance is indirect and uncertain.

The bill provides no funding or staffing plan for the Secretary of Health and Human Services to collect foreign price data annually and calculate an average for every drug and biological product, a large new administrative task.
A price cap on drugs sold in the U.S. reduces revenue for research-heavy drug companies, which opponents argue would mean less investment in developing new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and direct for people who pay list price, since American list prices are dramatically higher than prices for the same drugs in peer countries. The main costs fall on drugmakers, not on consumers, though the indirect effects on rebates and possible future drug development are legitimate concerns. The bill is short on implementation detail, and without enforcement funding its practical reach would depend heavily on regulations the executive branch would have to write.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew introduced the bill on May 13, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which has jurisdiction over prescription drug pricing.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill; there has been no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, since the price cap never advanced and U.S. list prices remain uncapped.

for.name: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred to it on the day of introduction; it has taken no further action, leaving the bill without a hearing or vote.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Major industry opposition to international reference pricing
against.what_they_did: Opposes international reference pricing schemes, which the industry has argued would import foreign government price controls and reduce funding for new drug development.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill and no one of either party cosponsored it, so no party positioning is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would force U.S. list prices down to the average of six other developed countries and fine violators ten times the overcharge per unit sold. Manufacturers would bear the cost of lower prices and of annual reporting on their prices in each country.

Rebates and negotiated discounts are commonly set relative to high U.S. list prices, so a list-price cap could shrink the spread that middlemen capture, but lower list prices could also be passed to consumers. The bill is silent on how rebates would change.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than months after introduction, the bill has no visible path forward. Most bills referred to committee without cosponsors or a hearing die at the end of the two-year Congress.
